statement: In laboratory tests, fentanyl test strips of different brands, production lots and ages did not perform the same, compared with the known content of prepared solutions. Lots: in one laboratory, two lots of one brand (BTNX Rapid Response, urine cut-off 20 ng/mL) obtained in 2017 detected fentanyl in water down to 20 ng/mL, while three lots obtained in 2021 detected it only down to 200 ng/mL, ten times higher, and in urine, the strips' intended use, down to 50–100 ng/mL; the 2021 lots also gave false positives with lidocaine, MDMA and diphenhydramine at concentrations 10 to 200 times lower, and with d-methamphetamine at a twofold higher one (editors' calculation on the study card). The two sets were tested in separate rounds (2017 and 2022), with storage and expiry not reported, so lot, storage and testing round cannot be separated (Halifax et al., 2024). Brands: on the same solutions, four brands detected 5 to 12 of 23 analogues at 100 ng/mL; one brand (One Step) read negative for carfentanil, sufentanil and benzodioxolefentanyl at every concentration, which the other three detected at higher concentrations, and it alone gave false positives with ascorbic acid at 10 mg/mL or more (Bergh et al., 2021). Heat and age: strips with a listed cut-off of 200 ng/mL detected 500 ng/mL whether or not they had been kept unopened at 55 °C for two weeks; strips of an older lot more than four years past expiry, kept in laboratory conditions, detected 250 ng/mL against their listed cut-off of 20 ng/mL, which is not less sensitive than the in-date strips in absolute terms (editors' comparison; Sisco et al., 2024b, one lot each, triplicates). In another laboratory, every strip in diphenhydramine solutions at 4 °C read positive at all three concentrations tried, with no fentanyl-free cold solution tested (Lockwood et al., 2021). How strips perform after storage as people keep them, after longer heat, or across many lots and brands was not measured. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: No. In laboratory tests, batches of one brand bought in 2021 needed ten times more fentanyl to show it than batches bought in 2017, and four brands differed in which related drugs they picked up. Two weeks of heat did not change one batch; strips more than four years out of date still worked but needed more fentanyl than their label said. Why batches differed could not be worked out from these studies.
population: Fentanyl, fentanyl analogues and other substances in water or drug-free urine, tested in laboratories
exposure: Fentanyl test strips of different brands (four), production lots (five lots of one brand, obtained in 2017 or 2021) and ages or storage (in date, kept unopened at 55 °C for two weeks, or more than four years past expiry); one test temperature of 4 °C
comparator: Known content of each solution, and the brands, lots and ages compared with each other
outcome: Lowest fentanyl concentration detected, analogue detection and false-positive thresholds
magnitude: Halifax et al.: fentanyl in water 20 ng/mL (2017 lots) against 200 ng/mL (2021 lots); in urine 50 and 100 ng/mL (2021 lots); false-positive thresholds 2017 against 2021 lots: d-methamphetamine 5 against 10, MDMA 50 against 2.5–5, lidocaine 100 against 2.5, diphenhydramine 100 against 0.5–1 mg/mL. Bergh et al.: analogues at 100 ng/mL 5, 5, 12 and 9 of 23 by brand; One Step negative for carfentanil, sufentanil and benzodioxolefentanyl at all concentrations; ascorbic acid false positives on One Step only. Sisco et al. (2024b): fentanyl strips 0.5 µg/mL heated or not (listed 0.2 µg/mL); expired fentanyl strips 0.25 µg/mL (listed 0.02 µg/mL); expired methamphetamine strips 5 against 1 µg/mL; expired cocaine strips unchanged at 2.5 µg/mL. Lockwood et al.: at 4 °C all diphenhydramine strips positive at 4, 2 and 1 mg/mL.

risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 high for Halifax et al. (lot comparison confounded with testing round and unreported storage) and Bergh et al. (post hoc, unblinded grading); Sisco et al. (2024b) has no instrument (editors' checklist, high) and compared expired strips with their labels rather than with fresh strips of the same lot; Lockwood et al.'s cold result had no blank.

inconsistency.note: No study contradicts another; each measured a different source of variation.

indirectness.note: Laboratory solutions read by trained staff; one brand's lots, four brands, and one lot each for heat and expiry; storage as people keep strips was not studied.

imprecision.note: Duplicate strips per concentration (Halifax et al.), single strips (Bergh et al.) and triplicates (Sisco et al., 2024b) at steps two- to fivefold apart, so differences of one step may be test-to-test variation; no repeatability was measured.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high; one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision gives very low. Rated as worded: that strips differed between brands, lots and ages in laboratory tests, not why they differed. Status replicated: independent laboratories found differences between brands (Bergh et al.) and between lots (Halifax et al.); the heat and expiry findings come from one in-vitro study.
